questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Sign convention for angular position
questions.learningObjective: assign a sign to angular position from the chosen positive sense
questions.stem: A wheel is observed from the right-hand end of its axle and is turning clockwise. Taking counterclockwise as the positive sense, what sign does its angular position carry?

options.text: Negative, because clockwise turning runs against the positive sense
Positive, because any complete turn counts as a positive angle
options.misconception: treats every rotation as positive no matter which sense was chosen

options.text: Zero, because the angle returns to its starting value after a full turn
options.misconception: believes the angle resets to zero each revolution, leaving no sign to assign

options.text: Positive, because clockwise is the standard positive sense for every observer
options.misconception: believes clockwise is the fixed positive direction regardless of the observer

questions.explanation: Angular position is a signed displacement, so its sign follows whichever sense the observer has declared positive. A wheel seen turning clockwise while counterclockwise is positive sweeps through negative angles, so its angular position is negative; the fact that a full turn returns to the same angle only means the position is 2 pi apart from its start, not that the sign is undefined.
questions.hint: Fix the positive sense first, then ask which way the wheel actually turns.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Angular displacement from revolution count
questions.learningObjective: convert a count of turns into angular displacement
questions.stem: A turntable makes 3.0 complete turns in the positive sense from its starting mark and then stops. What angular displacement in radians did it accumulate?
questions.explanation: One full turn is 2 pi radians, so 3.0 turns give 3.0 x 2 pi = 18.85 rad. Counting turns without converting loses the factor of 2 pi, and dividing instead of multiplying would give 0.212 rad, which is the angle per turn rather than the total.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of turns by 2 pi radians.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Origin of the rolling constraint
questions.learningObjective: explain why rolling without slipping fixes v equal to omega r
questions.stem: A wheel rolls along level ground without slipping. Why must the speed of the wheel's centre equal the product of its angular speed and its radius?

options.text: The point in contact with the ground is momentarily at rest, which fixes that product
Gravity on the contact point vanishes while the wheel is rolling
options.misconception: believes the contact point carries no weight so the constraint follows

options.text: The contact point travels at the same speed as the wheel's centre
options.misconception: believes the contact point moves along with the centre, doubling the relation

options.text: The rolling radius always equals the radius of the wheel's axle
options.misconception: assumes the axle and rolling radii must match for any wheel

questions.explanation: Rolling without slipping means the surfaces do not slide over each other, so the point of the rim touching the ground has zero instantaneous velocity. Since that point's velocity is the centre's velocity plus the rim contribution of magnitude omega r, the centre's speed must equal omega r exactly. The contact point is not a separate body, and nothing about axle radii enters the relation.
questions.hint: Look at the one point of the wheel that is not moving, and work backwards.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Moment of inertia as a sum over masses
questions.learningObjective: build a moment of inertia by summing mass times distance squared
questions.stem: A light rod of negligible mass carries three point masses: 0.50 kg at 0.20 m, 0.80 kg at 0.45 m and 0.30 kg at 0.60 m from the rotation axis. What is the total moment of inertia about that axis in kg.m^2?
questions.explanation: Each mass piece contributes m times d squared, so the total is 0.50 x 0.0400 = 0.0200, plus 0.80 x 0.2025 = 0.162, plus 0.30 x 0.360 = 0.108, giving 0.290 kg.m^2. Adding m x d instead would give 0.640 kg.m, which has the wrong units for a moment of inertia, and a bare sum of the masses would ignore distance altogether.
questions.hint: Square each distance first, then weight it by its mass.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Perpendicular-axis theorem for a lamina
questions.learningObjective: state the perpendicular-axis relation among the moments of a flat plate
questions.stem: A flat plate of uniform density rotates about an axis lying in the plate through its centre. How are its three relevant moments of inertia related?

options.text: The two in-plane moments add to give the moment about the perpendicular axis
Only the moment about the axis perpendicular to the plate can be found
options.misconception: believes in-plane moments of a plate are impossible to determine

options.text: The moment about any in-plane axis is half the perpendicular moment
options.misconception: believes an in-plane moment is always exactly half the perpendicular one

options.text: The three moments are independent and no relation links them
options.misconception: believes a lamina's moments obey no sum or difference law at all

questions.explanation: The perpendicular-axis theorem says that for a flat lamina the moment about an axis normal to the plane equals the sum of the moments about two mutually perpendicular in-plane axes through the same point. It is a sum, not a difference, and it holds only for flat plates, so a solid body such as a sphere cannot be treated this way.
questions.hint: The plate is flat, which is exactly the condition the theorem needs.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Rod inertia about its centre
questions.learningObjective: compute the moment of inertia of a rod about its centre
questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass 6.0 kg and length 1.20 m rotates about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to the rod. What is its moment of inertia in kg.m^2?

options.text: 0.72 kg.m^2 from the centre-of-mass form one twelfth ML squared
1.44 kg.m^2 from the form one half ML squared
options.misconception: applies the solid-disc coefficient to a rod instead of the rod's own form

options.text: 2.88 kg.m^2 from the form one third ML squared
options.misconception: uses the rod-about-one-end value while claiming a centre axis

options.text: 4.32 kg.m^2 from the form three fifths ML squared
options.misconception: borrows the solid-sphere coefficient and applies it to a rod

questions.explanation: A uniform rod about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its length has I = ML squared divided by twelve, which here is 6.0 x 1.44 divided by 12 = 0.72 kg.m^2. The one-third ML squared form applies only about an end, where every gram sits on average much farther out.
questions.hint: About the centre, not about the end, the coefficient is one twelfth.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Wheel driven by a hanging mass
questions.learningObjective: find the angular acceleration of a wheel driven by a falling weight
questions.stem: A uniform solid disc of mass 4.0 kg and radius 0.50 m turns about a fixed horizontal axle through its centre. A light string wound on its rim carries a hanging mass of 3.0 kg. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2 and ignoring axle friction, what is the disc's angular acceleration in rad/s^2?
questions.explanation: The hanging mass is not in free fall, so the string tension is less than its weight of 3.0 x 9.8 = 29.4 N. Solving mg minus T = m a with T r = I a divided by r for the disc of inertia one half M R squared = 0.50 kg.m^2 gives a = mg over m plus I over r squared = 29.4 over 3.0 plus 2.0, so a = 5.88 m/s^2 and alpha = a over r = 5.88 over 0.50 = 11.76 rad/s^2. Treating the tension as the full weight would wrongly give 29.4 rad/s^2.
questions.hint: Torque from the string's tension about the axle, then divide by the disc's inertia.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: String tension while a yo-yo unwinds
questions.learningObjective: compare the string tension on an unwinding yo-yo with its weight
questions.stem: A yo-yo hangs from a light string wrapped around its axle and unwinds as it falls. How does the string tension compare with the yo-yo's weight during the fall?

options.text: Smaller than the weight, because part of the pull goes into spinning the yo-yo
Equal to the weight, because the yo-yo stays in free fall throughout
options.misconception: believes any falling body is weightless along the string

options.text: Greater than the weight, because the string adds a downward pull as it unwinds
options.misconception: believes the unwinding string's pull adds to gravity instead of opposing it

options.text: Zero, because a string can only steer the motion and never pull
options.misconception: believes an unwinding string carries no tension at all

questions.explanation: The yo-yo accelerates downward but less than g, so the net force is less than its weight, which means the upward string tension is less than the weight. The missing part of the pull is not lost: it supplies the torque that spins the yo-yo up, and once the string is fully unwound the yo-yo does fall freely with tension near zero.
questions.hint: Compare the net force needed for the observed acceleration with the weight.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Power delivered by a torque
questions.learningObjective: compute rotational power from torque and angular speed
questions.stem: A wheel of moment of inertia 2.0 kg.m^2 is turned at a steady 6.0 rad/s by a constant torque of 4.0 N.m. What power in W does that torque deliver?
questions.explanation: Power in rotation is torque times angular speed, so 4.0 N.m x 6.0 rad/s = 24 W. Since both factors are steady there is no change of rotational energy to account for. Dividing instead would give 0.667 W, and quoting the torque alone would report 4.0 N.m, which is not a rate of doing work at all.
questions.hint: Power is the product of torque and angular speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Skater pulling in the arms
questions.learningObjective: predict the spin rate change when a skater pulls in the arms
questions.stem: A spinning skater with her arms extended draws both arms in tight against her body. How does her rate of spin change during the pull, and why?

options.text: It increases, because the same angular momentum in a smaller inertia needs more spin
It is unchanged, because angular momentum belongs to the skater whatever her shape
options.misconception: believes the conserved quantity fixes the spin rate rather than the momentum

options.text: It decreases, because pulling the arms in adds rotational inertia to the system
options.misconception: believes drawing mass inward always slows a spinner down

options.text: It is unchanged, because no external torque acts on her during the pull
options.misconception: believes zero external torque means the spin rate itself cannot change

questions.explanation: With negligible external torque the angular momentum I omega is held fixed. Pulling the arms in moves mass toward the axis and lowers I, so omega must rise in proportion, and the extra rotational kinetic energy is supplied by the work her muscles do. Zero net external torque constrains the momentum, not the spin rate, which is the trap in the last option.
questions.hint: Ask which of I and omega has to change when the body shape changes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Rotational second law statement
questions.learningObjective: state Newton's second law for rotation about a fixed axis
questions.stem: A reference sheet lists the laws of motion for a rigid body turning about a fixed axis. Which entry states the rotational second law correctly?

options.text: The net torque about the axis equals the moment of inertia times angular acceleration
The net torque about the axis equals the angular momentum times elapsed time
options.misconception: confuses torque with the rate of change of angular momentum

options.text: The net torque about the axis equals the mass times the angular velocity
options.misconception: pairs torque with linear quantities as though the body had no radius

options.text: The net torque about the axis equals the moment of inertia divided by the angle turned
options.misconception: treats torque as a ratio of inertia to displacement rather than a cause

questions.explanation: The rotational second law replaces force by net torque and mass by the moment of inertia, so the inertia plays the role of the body's resistance to angular acceleration. Torque divided by inertia gives angular acceleration; any statement that divides inertia by an angle has the wrong physical role for both quantities.
questions.hint: Match the linear law term by term: force becomes torque, mass becomes moment of inertia.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Acceleration of an unwinding yo-yo
questions.learningObjective: find the descent acceleration of a yo-yo with a fixed string end
questions.stem: A yo-yo of mass 0.40 kg and moment of inertia 1.6e-3 kg.m^2 hangs from a light string wound on an axle of radius 0.020 m whose free end is held fixed. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, what is the yo-yo's downward acceleration in m/s^2?
questions.explanation: Here I divided by M r squared is 1.6e-3 divided by 0.40 x 4.0e-4, which is 10, so the acceleration is g divided by 1 plus 10, namely 9.8 divided by 11 = 0.891 m/s^2. Answering g would be treating the yo-yo as freely falling, and treating the string tension as equal to the weight would wrongly cancel the spin-up torque.
questions.hint: The fixed string ties the axle's unwinding rate to the yo-yo's descent rate.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Direction of gyroscope precession
questions.learningObjective: state the sense of precession relative to the spin
questions.stem: A fast top is tilted from the vertical so that gravity supplies a torque about its contact point. In which sense does the top's symmetry axis precess, compared with the direction it is spinning?

options.text: In the same sense as the spin, ninety degrees away from the applied torque
In the sense opposite the spin, directly reversing the top's rotation
options.misconception: believes the gravitational torque simply reverses the spin direction

options.text: At right angles to the spin, out in the horizontal plane
options.misconception: believes the axis swings sideways, perpendicular to the precession sense

options.text: Not at all, because a vertical gravitational force cannot turn a horizontal axis
options.misconception: believes a purely vertical force produces no torque about the contact point

questions.explanation: The precession rate vector runs along torque crossed into the angular momentum, so a top spinning one sense precesses about the vertical in that same sense. Gravity is not the obstacle: its torque about the tilted contact point is real, and the top's large angular momentum is exactly what makes the response a slow sideways sweep rather than a fall.
questions.hint: Write the torque direction as the cross product of angular momentum and gravity.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a spinning wheel resists tipping
questions.learningObjective: explain why a rapidly spinning gyroscope does not tip over
questions.stem: A gyroscope spins rapidly about its horizontal axle while a torque tries to tip that axle toward the vertical. What does the gyroscope actually do while the torque acts?

options.text: Its axis swings sideways, at right angles to the applied torque, instead of tipping
Its axis tips over in the direction of the applied torque
options.misconception: believes a spinning body still tips straight toward the applied torque

options.text: It stops spinning and then tips over under the same torque
options.misconception: believes any applied torque first kills the spin and then topples it

options.text: Nothing moves, because a spinning body is immune to applied torque
options.misconception: believes a large spin rate makes the body completely torque-proof

questions.explanation: A large angular momentum along the axle means the torque can only change the direction of that momentum, not its size, so the response is a precessional swing perpendicular to the torque. The axle is not torque-proof: if the spin were slow the same torque would topple the gyroscope, which is why a stopped gyroscope falls over immediately.
questions.hint: Separate the magnitude of the angular momentum from its direction.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Spin-up from a reduced moment of inertia
questions.learningObjective: apply angular momentum conservation when inertia changes
questions.stem: A skater spinning at 4.0 rad/s with her arms out has a moment of inertia of 1.6 kg.m^2. She pulls her arms in, reducing that to 0.40 kg.m^2, with negligible external torque. What is her final angular speed in rad/s?
questions.explanation: Conservation of angular momentum gives I initial times omega initial = I final times omega final, so 1.6 x 4.0 = 6.4 kg.m^2/s, and dividing by the new inertia 0.40 gives 16 rad/s, four times the original rate. Holding the spin rate fixed instead would violate the conservation law outright.
questions.hint: Angular momentum, not spin rate, is the quantity that stays fixed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Friction direction when a wheel slips
questions.learningObjective: give the direction of kinetic friction for a slipping wheel
questions.stem: A cart's wheels are spinning too slowly for the cart's present speed, so the contact patch slides forward along the ground. In which direction does the friction force on the wheel point?

options.text: Backward, opposing the slide and speeding up the wheel's spin
Forward, pushing the cart along and dragging the wheel's spin down
options.misconception: believes friction always acts in the direction of motion

options.text: Absent, because two sliding surfaces generate no friction at all
options.misconception: believes sliding contact leaves the surfaces frictionless

options.text: Backward, and it also slows the wheel's spin as the cart moves on
options.misconception: believes backward friction must remove spin as well as push the cart back

questions.explanation: Kinetic friction always opposes the relative sliding of the two surfaces. Here the ground slides forward relative to the wheel, so the friction on the wheel points backward; because it acts at the rim, that backward push produces a torque in the same sense as the wheel's spin and speeds the rotation up until rolling without slipping is restored.
questions.hint: Friction opposes the slip of the surfaces, not the motion of the cart.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Energy comparison of a hoop and a disc
questions.learningObjective: compare rotational energies of bodies with the same mass and radius
questions.stem: A solid disc and a thin hoop each have mass 4.0 kg and radius 0.30 m, and both spin about their central axes at 5.0 rad/s. By how much in J does the hoop's rotational kinetic energy exceed the disc's?
questions.explanation: The disc has I = one half MR squared = 0.18 kg.m^2 and the hoop has MR squared = 0.36 kg.m^2. At 5.0 rad/s the energies are one half I omega squared, giving 2.25 J and 4.50 J, so the hoop exceeds the disc by 2.25 J. The gap exists because a hoop puts all of its mass at the full radius while a disc spreads the same mass over smaller radii.
questions.hint: With mass and radius matched, the two bodies differ only in how their inertia comes out.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Moment of inertia about a tangent line
questions.learningObjective: shift an axis to a tangent line with the parallel-axis theorem
questions.stem: A uniform solid disc of mass 5.0 kg and radius 0.30 m rolls about a horizontal axis that lies in the plane of the disc and is tangent to its rim. What is its moment of inertia about that tangent axis in kg.m^2?

options.text: 0.675 kg.m^2 from one half MR squared plus MR squared
0.225 kg.m^2 from the central axis value alone
options.misconception: omits the shift of the axis away from the centre of mass

options.text: 0.450 kg.m^2 from the shift term MR squared by itself
options.misconception: keeps only the translation term and drops the central inertia

options.text: 0.900 kg.m^2 from the axis taken along the rim's edge
options.misconception: treats the shift distance as the diameter rather than the radius

questions.explanation: The parallel-axis theorem gives I about the tangent line as one half MR squared plus M d squared with d equal to the radius, so 0.225 plus 0.450 gives 0.675 kg.m^2. The shift distance is one radius, not the diameter, and both the central term and the shift term are required.
questions.hint: The centre of the disc is one radius away from the tangent line.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Energy ranking at equal angular momentum
questions.learningObjective: rank rotational energies of rotors sharing an angular momentum
questions.stem: Three flywheels are spun so that each carries the same angular momentum of 8.0 kg.m^2/s: wheel A has I = 0.50 kg.m^2, wheel B has I = 2.0 kg.m^2 and wheel C has I = 4.0 kg.m^2. Rank their rotational kinetic energies from largest to smallest.

options.text: Wheel A, then wheel B, then wheel C
Wheel C, then wheel B, then wheel A
options.misconception: believes a larger moment of inertia stores more energy at fixed momentum

options.text: All three store the same rotational kinetic energy
options.misconception: assumes equal angular momentum guarantees equal rotational energy

options.text: Wheel B, then wheel A, then wheel C
options.misconception: ranks by inertia while ignoring the shared angular momentum

questions.explanation: Rewriting the energy as L squared divided by twice I shows it falls as the inertia grows, so with L = 8.0 the energies are 64 J, 16 J and 8 J for wheels A, B and C. Sharing an angular momentum does not mean sharing an energy, and ordering by inertia alone reverses the true ranking.
questions.hint: Express the energy in terms of angular momentum and inertia rather than spin rate.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Explaining gyroscope precession
questions.learningObjective: explain why a released spinning wheel does not simply fall over
questions.stem: A student holds a bicycle wheel by one end of its axle, spins it up, and lets go of the other support. The wheel does not drop; instead its axle turns in a slow circle. Explain what torque the spin produces and why the wheel behaves this way.

answer.exemplar: The wheel's weight pulls its centre of mass down, which is a torque about the held end that would ordinarily topple it. But the wheel also carries a large angular momentum along its axle, and a torque can only change the direction of that momentum, not its size, so the axle sweeps sideways around a cone. The precession rate is the torque divided by the spin angular momentum, so spinning faster makes the sweep slower and steadier rather than weaker.

questions.explanation: A full answer identifies the gravitational torque about the pivot, distinguishes it from a tipping torque, and uses the precession rate proportional to torque over angular momentum to explain why a faster spin gives a slower, steadier sweep. It should also note that the wheel is not free of torque, only protected by its large angular momentum.
questions.hint: Name the torque, then say which part of the motion it actually changes.

questions.stem: A turntable turns clockwise at 0.25 revolutions per second as seen from the front, where its label faces up. Taking counterclockwise as the positive sense, what is the signed angular velocity in rad/s?

Because the rotation is clockwise while counterclockwise is positive, the signed value is negative, so the answer is negative 1.571 rad/s. Reporting a positive number here ignores the agreed sense, which is exactly what the sign convention exists to prevent.

questions.topic: Linear and angular quantity pairs

options.text: Tangential speed equals angular speed times the radius from the axis
Tangential speed equals angular speed divided by the radius
options.misconception: divides by the radius when pairing angular and tangential speed

options.text: Centripetal acceleration equals angular speed times the radius
options.misconception: pairs centripetal acceleration with omega r instead of omega squared r

options.text: Tangential acceleration equals angular speed times the radius squared

questions.topic: Conditions on the parallel-axis theorem

Between any two axes at all, even ones in different directions

questions.topic: A spin claim that angular momentum forbids
questions.learningObjective: explain why a spin cannot be stopped without external torque
questions.stem: A student claims a spinning figure skater could bring the spin to an instant stop simply by holding perfectly still and doing nothing at all. Explain why conservation of angular momentum forbids this.

answer.exemplar: The skater's angular momentum I omega is fixed as long as the net external torque on her is negligible, and freezing still gives her no way to shed it: any change in her angular momentum would require a torque from outside her body. She can only change the spin by changing her moment of inertia, which trades omega against I without altering the product, or by pushing against something outside herself, which is a real external torque. Even a slow deliberate twist of the arms takes time, and during it the angular momentum simply moves between her body parts.

questions.explanation: A complete answer states that zero external torque fixes I omega, shows that still hands or a still body provide no way to reduce that product, and distinguishes the two permitted routes: reshaping the body, which only redistributes the same momentum, or an outside push, which supplies the torque that the claim denies.
questions.hint: Ask what supplies the torque that would have to change the angular momentum.

questions.hint: Sketch the two turns and check whether they reinforce or cancel.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Rotational share of a rolling body's energy
questions.learningObjective: separate the rotational and translational energy of a rolling cylinder
questions.stem: A solid cylinder of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.20 m rolls without slipping at 5.0 m/s. How many joules of its total kinetic energy are rotational?

options.text: 12.5 J, one third of the total, since the inertia is half M R squared
25.0 J, the same as the translational part, since mass sits at the rim
options.misconception: assumes a hoop's inertia and so puts all mass at the radius

options.text: 37.5 J, the entire kinetic energy of the rolling cylinder
options.misconception: reports the total energy as though it were all rotational

options.text: 8.33 J, a third of the total taken from the translational part
options.misconception: takes a fraction of the translational energy instead of the rotational share

questions.explanation: The rim speed makes the angular speed 25 rad/s, and with I = one half M R squared = 0.040 kg.m^2 the rotational energy is one half I omega squared = 12.5 J. The translational part is 25.0 J, so the total is 37.5 J and the rotational share is exactly one third, the signature of a solid cylinder rolling without slipping.
questions.hint: A solid cylinder rolling without slipping always splits its energy one third rotational.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Angular acceleration under opposing torques
questions.learningObjective: subtract a braking torque before dividing by the inertia
questions.stem: A wheel of moment of inertia 0.80 kg.m^2 is spun up by a driving torque of 6.0 N.m while a braking torque of 2.0 N.m acts against the same rotation. What angular acceleration in rad/s^2 results?

options.text: 5.0 rad/s^2 from the driving torque less the braking torque, over the inertia
10.0 rad/s^2 from adding the two torques before dividing by the inertia
options.misconception: adds a braking torque to the driving torque instead of subtracting

options.text: 2.5 rad/s^2 from the braking torque alone over the inertia
options.misconception: keeps only the resisting torque and discards the driving one

options.text: 1.25 rad/s^2 from dividing the inertia by the net torque
options.misconception: divides the inertia by the net torque, inverting the relation

questions.explanation: Torques in opposite senses subtract, so the net torque is 6.0 - 2.0 = 4.0 N.m and the angular acceleration is 4.0 divided by 0.80 = 5.0 rad/s^2. Adding the torques would predict the wheel speeds up faster with a brake fitted, and inverting the relation turns a torque into an acceleration of the wrong dimensions.
questions.hint: Net torque means signed sum, and braking opposes the rotation.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Which wheel spins up fastest
questions.learningObjective: compare spin-up rates from listed inertias and torques
questions.stem: A bench sheet lists three wheels of equal radius 0.30 m: wheel A with I = 0.45 kg.m^2 under a torque of 1.8 N.m, wheel B with I = 0.30 kg.m^2 under the same 1.8 N.m, and wheel C with I = 0.30 kg.m^2 under a torque of 0.9 N.m. Which spins up fastest, and at what angular acceleration?

options.text: Wheel A, at 4.0 rad/s^2, because it carries the largest torque share
options.misconception: judges by the driving torque alone without dividing by the inertia

options.text: Wheel B, at 6.0 rad/s^2, because its inertia and torque combine best
Wheel C, at 3.0 rad/s^2, because it carries the smallest inertia
options.misconception: judges by the smallest inertia without reading the torque paired with it

options.text: Wheel B, at 1.8 rad/s^2, because the torque is the spin-up rate
options.misconception: reports the driving torque as though it were the angular acceleration

questions.explanation: Angular acceleration is torque over inertia, giving 1.8 over 0.45 = 4.0 rad/s^2 for A, 1.8 over 0.30 = 6.0 rad/s^2 for B and 0.9 over 0.30 = 3.0 rad/s^2 for C, so B responds fastest. B and C share an inertia yet differ in rate, and B and A share a torque yet differ in rate, which is why neither column alone settles the question.
questions.hint: Divide each listed torque by the inertia paired with it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Inertia is set by mass distribution alone
questions.learningObjective: explain what determines a body's moment of inertia
questions.stem: A student asks why a wheel's moment of inertia has the same value whether the wheel is barely creeping or spinning quickly. Which statement gives the correct reason?

options.text: The inertia is fixed by how the mass is distributed about the axis
The inertia grows with speed, so a fast wheel has proportionally more
options.misconception: believes the moment of inertia increases as the spin rate rises

options.text: The inertia falls with speed, so a fast wheel is easier to redirect
options.misconception: believes the moment of inertia decreases as the spin rate rises

options.text: The mass itself shifts outward as the wheel speeds up
options.misconception: believes a rigid wheel's mass distribution changes with its speed

questions.explanation: The moment of inertia sums mass times distance squared, so it depends only on the body's geometry and its axis, both of which are unchanged by spinning it. Speed enters the rotational second law through angular acceleration, not through the inertia, which is why a wheel's response to a given torque does not change with how fast it is already turning.
questions.hint: Look at the definition and ask which symbols in it involve motion.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why the full weight is not the tension
questions.learningObjective: explain why a falling weight's full weight is not the tension on a driven wheel
questions.stem: A hanging weight drives a wheel through a string wound on the wheel's rim. Why can the string's tension not simply be set equal to the weight every time?

options.text: The weight's pull is split between accelerating the weight and spinning the wheel up
The tension is always equal to the wheel's own weight instead
options.misconception: believes the tension is set by the wheel's weight rather than by the pull

options.text: The string carries no tension while the wheel is being spun up
options.misconception: believes the tension is zero for the whole of the spin-up

options.text: The weight is lighter near the ground where the wheel is hung
options.misconception: believes local gravity changes as a mass descends a little

questions.explanation: If the tension equalled the weight the hanging mass would have no net force and could not accelerate, so some of the pull must go into building the falling mass's speed as well as into the torque that spins the wheel. The smaller the wheel's inertia, the larger the share going into spin-up and the closer the tension comes to the full weight.
questions.hint: Ask what the falling mass's net force would be if the tension equalled its weight.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Formula for rotational kinetic energy
questions.learningObjective: state the formula for a body's rotational kinetic energy
questions.stem: A spinner turns about a fixed axis and its whole motion is rotation about that axis. Which expression gives its rotational kinetic energy?

options.text: One half I omega squared, with I the inertia about the axis
One half m v squared, with v the speed of the centre of mass
options.misconception: uses the translational formula and leaves out the spin entirely

options.text: I omega squared, with I the inertia about the axis
options.misconception: drops the one-half factor that comes from the integration

options.text: One half I omega, with I the inertia about the axis
options.misconception: uses the angular speed instead of its square

questions.explanation: The rotational energy mirrors the translational one half m v squared with inertia replacing mass and angular speed replacing linear speed, giving one half I omega squared. The centre-of-mass speed contributes nothing here because a body turning about a fixed axis has a stationary centre, and the square on omega is not optional since speed builds up gradually during a spin-up.
questions.hint: Translate the linear energy formula word for word into rotation.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Torque as the rate of change of angular momentum
questions.learningObjective: state torque as the rate of change of angular momentum
questions.stem: A study card lists statements about how torque relates to the motion of a rotating body. Which one is correct?

options.text: The net external torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum
The net external torque equals inertia times angular velocity
options.misconception: multiplies the inertia by the spin rate instead of the angular acceleration

options.text: The net external torque equals angular momentum times the angle turned
options.misconception: multiplies angular momentum by an angle instead of differentiating in time

options.text: The net external torque equals the sum of the individual torque magnitudes
options.misconception: adds the magnitudes of opposed torques instead of their signed net

questions.explanation: The rate of change of angular momentum is a torque, and this holds whether or not the body's inertia is constant, which is what makes it the more general of the two statements. Inertia times angular velocity is a product of two quantities rather than a rate of change of anything, and opposed torques must be summed as signed quantities so that they can cancel.
questions.hint: Ask which statement would survive if the body's inertia changed with time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a yo-yo falls more slowly than a block
questions.learningObjective: explain why a descending yo-yo accelerates less than g
questions.stem: A yo-yo and a loose block of the same mass are dropped from the same height with the yo-yo's string end held fixed. The block reaches the floor first. Explain why, and say which property of the yo-yo makes the difference largest.

answer.exemplar: The block is in free fall the whole way, so it gains speed at exactly g. The yo-yo's held string stops it from falling freely: the string tension acts upward, and part of the string's pull goes into torque that spins the yo-yo up rather than into speeding up its descent. Its acceleration is therefore g divided by one plus I over M r squared, so a yo-yo with a large inertia compared with M r squared, which means most of its mass sits far from the axle, is the slowest. A yo-yo wound on a thin axle has little spin-up cost and falls closest to free fall.

questions.explanation: A full answer ties the smaller acceleration to the upward string tension, explains that the missing pull is spent as torque spinning the yo-yo up, and uses the acceleration formula to show that the inertia relative to M r squared is what sets how much of the weight is diverted into spin.
questions.hint: Compare the two free-body diagrams and account for the missing pull.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a rim does not fly off a spinning wheel
questions.learningObjective: explain why rim elements stay attached to a spinning wheel
questions.stem: A student watches a wheel spinning fast and says the rim must be flung outward by a centrifugal force, so it should eventually fly apart. Explain why the rim stays on the wheel instead.

answer.exemplar: There is no outward force on the rim in the ground's frame. Each element of the rim is continually pulled inward by the tension and compression in the material of the wheel, and that inward force is precisely what bends its path into a circle at constant speed. A force is needed to change the direction of the velocity, not to sustain the magnitude, and an element whose inward pull stopped would simply fly off in a straight line along its tangent. The outward push that appears in a rotating frame is a bookkeeping device, real only inside that frame, and it balances the inward pull without ever being what holds the rim on.

questions.explanation: A complete answer denies the outward force as a real interaction, names the inward force supplied by the wheel's material, and connects that inward force to the bending of the rim element's path rather than to any speeding up. It should also say what the rotating-frame outward force is, since that is the belief being corrected.
questions.hint: Ask what force is actually required to keep a rim element in a circle.
